name: Network security in a VPC: network ACLs and security groups

lesson.summary: Two components control traffic in a VPC. A network ACL is a firewall at the subnet level. It is stateless and checks inbound and outbound traffic against allow and deny rules. A security group is a firewall attached to an instance. It is stateful, so return traffic for an allowed request is permitted automatically, and it holds only allow rules. Securing these components is the customer's responsibility under the shared responsibility model.
keyPoints: A network ACL controls traffic at the subnet level and is stateless, so return traffic must be allowed explicitly
Network ACLs can contain both allow and deny rules
A security group controls traffic for an instance such as an EC2 instance and is stateful
Security groups only contain allow rules, and by default they deny all inbound traffic and allow all outbound traffic
Use security groups for fine-grained control of individual instances and network ACLs for broad control of a subnet
The customer configures network ACLs and security groups, so they are part of the customer's security responsibility

scenarios.text: A retail customer runs several EC2 instances in a public subnet. The application needs many different rules for traffic to each instance, and the team wants to apply them per instance.

questions.prompt: Which feature should the team use to set traffic rules for each instance?

options.text: Security groups attached to the EC2 instances
Changing the public subnet to a private subnet

questions.explanation: Security groups are attached to instances and provide fine-grained traffic rules per instance. Changing the subnet type would remove the public access the application needs, and a virtual private gateway and passwords do not filter traffic per instance.

questions.prompt: Which component performs stateless packet filtering at the subnet level?

options.text: A network access control list (network ACL)

questions.explanation: A network ACL filters packets crossing a subnet border and does not remember earlier requests, which makes it stateless. A security group is stateful, and a VPC or subnet does not filter packets on its own.

questions.prompt: A customer wants broad control of traffic in and out of a subnet and needs both allow and deny rules. Which solution fits best?

options.text: Security groups, which only hold allow rules
Changing the subnet to a public subnet

questions.explanation: Network ACLs control traffic at the subnet level and support both allow and deny rules. Security groups only hold allow rules, and the other two options do not control subnet traffic.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about security groups are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: They are stateful, so return traffic for an allowed request is permitted automatically
They are stateless and must allow return traffic explicitly
They attach to instances such as EC2 instances

questions.explanation: Security groups are stateful and attach to instances. They only hold allow rules, and stateless behaviour describes network ACLs.

questions.statement: Configuring network traffic protection for the resources in your VPC is the customer's responsibility under the shared responsibility model.
questions.explanation: True. AWS secures the underlying infrastructure, while the customer is responsible for network traffic protection for its own resources, such as configuring security groups.
